titulo.texto: The Tlamanaliztli Altar / Communal Offering of the Tender Corn

frase_gancho.texto: An altar of tender corn to give thanks for the harvest and call the rain.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the corn altar we move on to another way of asking for rain: dance. Look for masks with exaggerated features, clothing of rough cloth, and the whips of the dancers from Guerrero known as tlacololeros.

guion_corto.texto: This altar is a Nahua offering called Tlamanaliztli, a Nahuatl word that could be translated as “the act of making an offering.” It is made to give thanks for the harvest and to ask that the rains not fail. Notice what it is made of: arches of cornstalk and yellow pericón flowers, tender ears of corn, husks and all, corn tamales, atole, clay pots of mole, and incense burners with smoking copal. The idea is simple: the first thing the earth gives is offered before it is eaten. In the ceremony, the wise elders of the community pray in Nahuatl, and afterward everyone shares the food. It is a way of saying thank you to the earth and to the water.

guion_largo.texto:
Ending the tour with an ear of fresh corn is no accident. Since the first villages, corn has accompanied every hall: the villages of Tlatilco cultivated it, it fed great Teotihuacán, the Maya asked Chaac for it, and the peoples you saw upstairs still tend it in the milpa. Here you see it at its most tender and most celebrated moment, when it is still a green ear.

Words have a history too. Elote comes from the Nahuatl elotl, and jilote, the ear that has barely formed, comes from xilotl. The word milpa comes from milli, “sown field,” and pan, “in.” That is to say, every time you speak of tender corn or of the field that gives it, you are using the language of the Mexica without realizing it.

The Mexica had a goddess of tender corn, Xilonen, whose name is related to the jilote. Her festival fell in the season of the first ears of corn. It is thought that from that tradition come gestures that are still alive: not eating the new corn without first offering it, giving thanks, and sharing it. When you look at this altar, you may be seeing a custom that spans more than five hundred years.

Look at how it is put together. The arch, which you already saw in the [Xantolo altar](mna_s18_altar_xantolo), returns here, made of cornstalk and flowers. Pericón, a yellow flower that smells of anise, is the one used in open-air offerings, and it is said to protect against bad airs. The corn tamales, the atole, and the mole are festive foods. And the copal rises toward the sky, as in the [Lacandon incense burner](mna_s19_incensario_lacandon): once again, smoke as a message.

Those who lead the ceremony, traditional sages called tlamatque, speak with the spirits of the water, the tlaloque. According to the Mexica, these helpers of Tláloc kept the rain in great jars and broke them with rods so that it would fall, and thunder was the sound of the blows. This is the same Tláloc as the [monolith that welcomed you](mna_s00_monolito_tlaloc) at the entrance of the museum, and whom you saw under other names in Oaxaca and among the Maya.

Think of the three ways of asking for water that you have seen: the Cha Chaak of the Maya, the yúmari of the Rarámuri, and this Tlamanaliztli of the Nahua Peoples. The names, the songs, and the food change, but not the intention. In a country where the milpa depends on the rains, asking and giving thanks are part of living.

The offering is prepared by many people. Some bring the corn, others grind it, others prepare the tamales, and afterward the food is shared among everyone. It is the same spirit as the tequio you learned about in the first hall upstairs, and as the Otomi stewardships: nobody receives alone. What is not left on the altar is eaten among the community, and so gratitude becomes celebration.

If there is one idea that sums up this museum, it may be this: the people who live on this land have always known how to give thanks for what they receive. From the rain to the corn and from the corn to the word, that is the thread. Two stops remain in this hall: a dance and a garment with a legendary reputation.

texto: Look for the arch of cornstalk and yellow flowers
Count how many ears of corn with their husks are on the altar
Imagine the aroma of the copal, the pericón, and the corn tamales

texto.Region: Northern Sierra of Puebla, Guerrero, State of Mexico and Huasteca
texto.Technique/Material: Maize (fresh ears of corn), marigold, copal, clay, cut-paper banners, bread and candles
texto.Function: Agricultural ritual altar of thanksgiving for the harvest and sacred veneration of maize

texto.pregunta: Myth: Corn offerings are just decoration.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They are a ceremony of thanksgiving and petition: the first corn is offered before it is eaten, and the food is shared among everyone.
